State
stāt
n. (condition; standing; the settled circumstances of a man, a flock, a house or a land)
Latin status, from stare, to stand — the way a thing stands. In the Authorized Version state is never the modern political abstraction; it is the condition a person or people is actually in, and Scripture is always concerned that it be honestly known.

Biblical Definition

Two verses govern this word. First David's measure of a man: “Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity” (Psa 39:5). Not at his worst — at his best state, in the fullness of health, standing and success, a man is a breath. That is the honest reckoning from which all Christian ambition must begin. Second, Solomon's charge to the man responsible for others: “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds” (Pro 27:23). It is a farmer's proverb and has always been read as a pastor's and a father's. Oversight is not a title but an actual knowledge of the actual condition of those in one's charge, sheep by sheep. Proverbs adds the political form: “For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged” (Pro 28:2). And our Lord gives the most sobering use: of the man swept and garnished from whom the unclean spirit went out and returned with seven worse, “the last state of that man is worse than the first” (Mat 12:45). Reformation without regeneration leaves a house empty and available.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines state as condition, the circumstances of a being or thing at any given time; and also rank, condition of life, and a political body.

expand to see more

STATE, n. Condition; the circumstances of a being or thing at any given time.

1. Situation; condition; as, to be in a state of health or of sickness.

2. Rank; condition; quality; as the state of a nobleman.

3. Pomp; appearance of greatness; as, to be received in state.

4. A political body, or body politic; the whole body of people united under one government.

Key Scripture

Psa 39:5 — "Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah."

Pro 27:23 — "Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds."

Mat 12:45 — "Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first. Even so shall it be also unto this wicked generation."

Pro 28:2 — "For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged."

Modern Corruption

Moral improvement is offered where regeneration is needed; our Lord says the swept house ends in a worse state than it began.

expand to see more

Matthew 12:45 is the standing rebuke of every programme of reformation that stops short of the new birth. The house is swept and garnished — genuinely cleaner than it was, the obvious vice put out, the life visibly tidied — and it is empty. What returns is seven spirits worse than the first, and the last state of that man is worse than the first. Recovery programmes, moral crusades and behaviour-management discipleship can all produce a swept house. Only Christ can occupy it. This is precisely why the Reformed order puts regeneration first: a nature must be changed, not merely a conduct corrected.

The second thing to recover is Proverbs 27:23, which cuts against how oversight is now commonly exercised. Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks assumes a shepherd who can tell you, sheep by sheep, how each one is — and the verse goes on to say that riches are not for ever, and doth the crown endure to every generation? Position is temporary; knowledge of the flock is the work. An elder who knows the budget, the platform and the metrics but could not say which of his members is in trouble this month has the title without the office.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew matsab (H4673), a station, standing place; panim (H6440), face, condition; Greek eschatos (G2078), last — the last state.

expand to see more

Hebrew matsab (H4673) — a station, a post, a standing; Isaiah 22:19, from thy state shall he pull thee down.

Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, appearance, condition; Proverbs 27:23, the face of thy flocks — how they actually look.

Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, breath, vanity; Psalm 39:5, every man at his best state.

Greek eschatos (G2078) — last, final; Matthew 12:45, Luke 11:26, the last state of that man.

Greek scholazo (G4980) — to be at leisure, to stand empty; Matthew 12:44, the house found empty, swept and garnished.

Usage

"“Every man at his best state is altogether vanity” — at his best."

"“Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” — sheep by sheep."

"“The last state of that man is worse than the first” — a swept, empty house."
